notes.meaning: The Lord told Moses to command Aaron's sons not to make themselves ritually unclean by touching a dead body. In Israel, touching a corpse made a person unclean for a whole week, which would keep a priest from serving at the tabernacle. God set priests apart for holy service, so they were to stay close to life and far from death.

God made an exception for the priest's closest family members, including his mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and unmarried virgin sister. Since an unmarried sister still lived in her father's house, her brother had the duty to arrange her burial. In His mercy, the Lord allowed ordinary priests to express natural love and mourn for their nearest kin.

A priest was not allowed to make himself ceremonially unclean for distant relatives or people related to him only by marriage. Doing so would bring dishonor on his sacred role as a leader and make him unfit for God's work. Leaders among God's people were called to maintain their spiritual readiness at all times.

Priests were forbidden to practice pagan mourning customs, such as shaving bald spots on their heads, trimming the edges of their beards, or cutting their skin. Surrounding heathen nations used these harsh rituals to show extreme, hopeless grief for the dead. God's ministers were to display calm trust and self-control, showing faith rather than despair.

Priests were required to stay holy because they placed the food offerings on the Lord's altar, which was treated as God's table. If a priest became unclean, he would bring shame on God's holy name and disrupt the worship of the community. Serving in the Lord's presence demanded outward purity and complete dedication.

An ordinary priest was not allowed to marry a prostitute, an unchaste woman, or a woman divorced from her husband. A priest had to lead the community by setting a godly example in his own home and family life. His marriage needed to be above suspicion so that no scandal would touch his holy office.

The people of Israel were instructed to treat each priest with deep respect and regard him as holy. Because the priest carried out the sacred worship on behalf of the nation, the community had to hold him to God's high standard. God reminded His people that He is the holy Lord who sets them apart.

If a priest's daughter turned to prostitution, she dishonored her father and brought public shame upon his sacred role. Because she was raised in a home dedicated to God's worship, her sin brought great contempt upon religion itself. Her severe punishment of execution followed by burning showed how dangerous it was to bring disgrace upon God's sanctuary.

The high priest was distinguished from all other priests because the holy anointing oil had been poured on his head and he wore special sacred garments. He was forbidden from letting his hair hang loose or tearing his clothes as signs of mourning. Because he stood as the chief representative between God and the nation, he could not show signs of brokenness during his holy duties.

The high priest was forbidden from going near any dead body, even if it was his own mother or father. Common priests could attend the funerals of parents, but the high priest could not contract seven days of defilement without leaving the whole nation without its chief intercessor. His duty to God and the people came before his private family bonds.

The high priest was not to abandon the tabernacle during his sacred duties to run out to a funeral, which would dishonor the sanctuary. The holy anointing oil upon him marked him as entirely consecrated to the Lord's presence. God required him to show that his sacred calling took precedence over all earthly grief.

The high priest was allowed to marry only a virgin from his own people, the nation of Israel. Unlike common priests who could marry a widow, the high priest could not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or any woman of ill repute. This strict standard ensured that the line of future high priests had an unquestioned, pure heritage.

Following these marriage laws protected the high priest's children from being disqualified from the priesthood. If he had married an unlawful wife, his sons would have been barred from stepping into the sacred office after him. The Lord, who sets the high priest apart, guarded the holiness of the family line.

The Lord instructed Moses to tell Aaron that no priest with a physical defect could approach the altar to offer sacrifices. Just as animal sacrifices had to be physically unblemished, the officiating priest had to be whole and without defect. This rule pointed toward the complete perfection of Christ, the true High Priest to come.

The Lord gave a list of specific physical defects that disqualified a priest from serving at the altar, including blindness, lameness, facial disfigurement, broken limbs, and skin diseases. In the ancient world, physical wholeness stood as a visible picture of spiritual health and reverence. These physical rules kept the public worship of the sanctuary free from distraction or disrespect.

Any descendant of Aaron who had a physical defect was barred from bringing the burnt offerings and the sacred food to the altar. Even if he was a godly man with great knowledge, his outward blemish prevented him from performing the sacrifice. God maintained high visual standards to remind Israel of His supreme perfection.

A priest with a physical defect was still permitted to eat the holy and most holy portions of the sacrifices provided for Aaron's family. A physical disability was not a moral sin, so he remained a true member of the priestly house and enjoyed God's caring provision. God showed great compassion by feeding and honoring the man even while setting limits on his public service.

The blemished priest was not permitted to enter the holy place before the inner veil or approach the bronze altar outside. This restriction protected the sacred spaces of the tabernacle from being treated as ordinary. God reaffirmed that He is the Lord who makes His sanctuaries holy.

Moses faithfully shared all of these rules with Aaron, his sons, and the entire nation of Israel. The priests needed to know how to guard their purity, and the people needed to know which priests were qualified to offer their sacrifices. The whole community worked together to preserve the honor of God's house.
